headline: Equinox Tides Empty the River — Bunker Pour Past Saybrook Point, Stripers Stack the Mouth
subhead: The Harvest Moon is pulling bait out of the Connecticut River faster than it has all season, and the bass know it.
body_markdown:
The equinox always marks the turn on this river. The marsh grass at Great Island is starting to go from green to that dull gold it wears through October, the ospreys are mostly gone off the nest platforms, and the bunker that spent the summer working up into the coves off Essex and Old Lyme are now pointed the other way — down and out, riding the outgoing tide toward the Sound. That's the signal that matters most right now. Not the calendar. The bait movement.

This week the Harvest Moon put some real muscle behind the tides, and a bigger swing means more water moving faster through the mouth twice a day. Every ebb is pulling a heavier volume of peanut and adult menhaden out past the jetties at Saybrook Point, and the stripers have figured out exactly where to sit and wait for it. We flagged this pattern last week — said striper numbers would build steadily as the seasonal push accelerated — and that's exactly what's showing up at the river mouth now. The bass aren't scattered through the system anymore. They're stacking tight to structure right where the current funnels.

The better bite this week has been on the last three hours of the outgoing, from the range lights down through the rock piles off Saybrook Point and out toward the Old Saybrook breakwater. That's where the bait gets squeezed into a chute and the bass don't have to work for it. Boats working topwater at first light have had good luck with bone or bunker-colored Doc poppers and 7-inch Super Spooks worked over the surface disturbance — when bunker start dimpling or nervous-watering ahead of a push of fish, that's the tell to cast into it rather than past it. Once the sun gets up and the surface bite backs off, guys are dropping bunker-imitation soft plastics — 6-inch white or bunker-pattern paddletails on 1- to 2-ounce jigheads — down into the deeper cuts along the Lynde Point side, letting them swing with the current instead of retrieving hard against it.

Great Island continues to hold juvenile bass and some slot fish working the flats and channel edges on the tail of the ebb, though that bite has been more of a sunrise-and-dusk affair than an all-day proposition. Small bucktails, half-ounce to three-quarter, tipped with a strip of fresh bunker belly, have out-produced straight plastic on the flats when the water's got some clarity to it after a stretch of settled weather. When the wind kicks up out of the southwest, as it's done a few afternoons this week, the flats go from fishable to frustrating fast — that chop stirs the shallow mud bottom and the sight-feeding bite shuts down until it clears.

Bluefish have been riding along with the bunker schools the same way they always do this time of year, and that push has been building noticeably around the mouth over the past several days. Snapper-sized fish are thick in the coves off Old Lyme, but there's been a mix of larger blues — two to four pounds — chopping through the same bait pods the stripers are working near the jetties. If you're throwing topwater for bass and getting your plug shredded, that's not bad luck, that's the second wave of predators showing up on schedule. Wire leader or a heavier fluorocarbon shock leader isn't optional right now if you want to keep your good lures.

White perch have gone quiet the way they typically do once the water starts cooling and the bigger predators move in — worth a mention only because a few reports have come in of incidental perch mixed with school bass up around the DEP Marina stretch on small grubs, but nobody's targeting them seriously this week and shouldn't be.

The broader Sound picture backs up what's happening at the mouth. Water out toward the western Sound has been sitting in the low 70s, with a noticeable cooling trend moving east — and that gradient is exactly what pushes bait and predators to concentrate rather than spread thin. As the river itself starts shedding its summer warmth over the next couple weeks, expect that concentration effect to sharpen right here at the confluence, where river water meets Sound water and bait has nowhere to hide.

Looking at the next few days: if the wind stays out of the north or northwest and lays down overnight, the dawn topwater window at Saybrook Point and the breakwater should hold up, maybe even improve as more bait gets flushed on these bigger tides. If a southwest blow returns and roughs up the flats again, shift effort to the deeper current seams along Lynde Point and fish subsurface rather than chasing surface commotion that won't show. Either way, the pattern is only going one direction from here — more bass, more bait, tighter to the mouth — right through the next couple weeks as the fall push builds toward its peak.
